draftPackage.topic: Devils Hole and the distant Kamchatka earthquake
draftPackage.centralQuestion: How did an earthquake thousands of miles away make waves in a Nevada desert cave?
draftPackage.thesis: Passing seismic motion can set local enclosed water oscillating; a modest physical disturbance can affect the shallow shelf of an apparently isolated habitat.
draftPackage.viewerPayoff: Explain the distant-earthquake/local-water connection and its limited, real ecological consequence.

sources.organization: National Park Service / Death Valley National Park
sources.title: Russian earthquake causes minor disturbance in Devils Hole
sources.notes: Direct site-operator event report and biological interpretation. Authoritative for local observations, not an independent analysis of raw monitoring data. Distance, delay and wave size are reported NPS values. Amplitude convention and raw onset series are absent; no universal seismic speed is derived. December/February ecological effects and the March count of 38 fish are separate observations and unused. The before image bears July 14, 2025; the after image July 30. They are not immediately adjacent observations or a quantitative mortality comparison.

sources.organization: U.S. Geological Survey / Earthquake Hazards Program
sources.title: Seismic Seiches
sources.notes: Established mechanism from the relevant scientific agency. A different institution from NPS, not independent replication of July 2025 cave monitoring. General physics, not a calculated Devils Hole normal mode, calibrated amplitude or exact propagation path. No one-path model or claim that distance alone determines local wave height.

draftAsset.editorialPurpose: Explain the distant-earthquake/local-water connection and its limited, real ecological consequence.
draftAsset.storyAngle: An isolated-looking pool responds to a remote earthquake through seismic motion, with a modest consequence for a vulnerable habitat.

segments.text: An earthquake nearly four thousand miles away made waves in this Nevada desert pool.
On July twenty-ninth, twenty twenty-five, a magnitude eight point eight quake struck off Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula.
Twenty-one minutes later, water in Devils Hole began sloshing.
But seawater hadn’t crossed the ocean into Nevada.
Seismic waves traveled through the ground.
As the ground moved, water already inside the cave rocked back and forth—like water in a shaken bathtub.
That oscillation is called a seismic seiche, different from an ocean tsunami.
The waves here were about ten inches.
Small, but enough to disturb a shallow shelf where the endangered Devils Hole pupfish feed and spawn.
This event removed some material from the shelf. The park described it as a minor disturbance.
An isolated-looking pool can reveal just how connected the ground beneath us really is.

misconceptionSafeguards: Energy propagation and water displacement are distinct. No ocean-water path or subterranean channel from Russia to Nevada.
Distant forcing is represented by qualitative seismic surface-motion cues; no ray through Earth’s core, calibrated travel speed or human-perceptible shaking at the cave.
Date context is July29 Nevada/UTC, July30 Kamchatka local. No invented exact cave-arrival timestamp from a rounded interval.
Ten inches is a reported event value with unspecified height convention. No universal seiche size, metre-scale July wave or magnitude-equals-local-intensity claim.
Shelf dependence and limited July material loss are distinct from previous disturbances, extinction risk estimates and current population.
NPS before/after frames bear July14 and July30; not adjacent observations, a mortality test or a measured removal ratio.
An ocean tsunami can also have been generated by this earthquake; its existence does not make the cave waves a tsunami.
All new illustrations must identify schematic geometry/motion and reconstruction; source photos are consultation-only.
review.comprehensionReview: First frame links a recognizable dry-rock pool to a distant earthquake without waiting for generic establishing footage. Event numbers appear sequentially. Existing water remains continuous as ground motion is separated and translated into rocking. The term seiche follows the visual causal explanation; the feeding shelf becomes meaningful only afterward. Ending resolves the connected-Earth idea. Actual first-frame clarity, caption density and pacing need future rendered review; no audience panel conducted.
review.rightsReview: Original geographic/cave/shelf illustrations selected conceptually. Three NPS-credited reference photos were inspected ephemerally under the published government-work policy, with asset URLs/hashes/credits retained; none imported for production. No monitoring video viewed or audio copied, no protected logo or source image selected. Established Manrope and af_heart remain proposed; record licenses and canonical identities for actual future assets when authorized.

careAssessment.rationale: Historical geophysical explanation with inspected operator evidence and corroborating scientific-agency mechanisms/catalog. No medical advice, exceptional cost, rights exception or brand deviation. Unselected exact resonance and exaggerated impact claims are excluded from the artifact.
